results.title: Pythagoras' Theorem: Free GCSE Maths Lesson & Worksheet
excerpts:
Step-by-step method for Pythagoras’ Theorem
1. Sketch the right-angled triangle and mark the right angle.
2. Label the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle) as c , and the other sides as a and b .
3. Substitute into a² + b² = c². Rearrange if a shorter side is missing.
4. Calculate carefully on a calculator, then round to the required accuracy.
Quick reference: finding the hypotenuse vs a shorter side
Finding the hypotenuse
c = \sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2}}
Best for: both shorter sides known.
Finding a shorter side
a = \sqrt{c^{2} - b^{2}}
Best for: hypotenuse and one other side known.
⚠️ Common mistakes
* ❌ Calling the wrong side the hypotenuse. It must be opposite the right angle.
* ❌ Adding instead of subtracting when a shorter side is missing. Use c² − b².
* ❌ Forgetting to square root after finding a² + b².
* ❌ Rounding too early. Keep full calculator values until the final step.
Proving Pythagoras’ Theorem
There are many proofs of Pythagoras’ Theorem.
My favourite classroom approach is to cut out four congruent right-angled triangles of base b and height a . Arrange them to form a square whose side length is the hypotenuse c .
Students find the area of the large square in two ways: as c ², and as the four triangles plus the inner square.
* Starter: show a right-angled triangle and ask students to point to the hypotenuse before any calculation.
* Support: begin with integer Pythagorean triples so the square-root step lands cleanly.
* Challenge: set composite perimeter problems where Pythagoras unlocks one missing edge first.
* Common fix: if students use a² + b² = c² with the wrong side as c , ask them to mark the right angle and draw an arrow to the opposite side.

* The area of a triangle is calculated by finding the length of the base, halving it, and then multiplying it by the perpendicular height.

results.title: Triangle Area Formula — All 5 Ways to Find Area (½bh, Heron's & More)
excerpts:
* | ½ × base × height formula | Heron's formula
* Formula | A = ½ b h | A = √[s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)]
* Information needed | A base length and its perpendicular height | All three side lengths
* When to use | When the height is known or easy to find | When only side lengths are available and the height is unknown
* Complexity | Simple multiplication | Requires computing the semiperimeter, then a square root
Common Mistakes
Mistake: Forgetting to multiply by ½ and computing base × height as the full area.
Correction: Always remember that a triangle is half a parallelogram. The correct formula is A = ½ × b × h, not b × h.
Mistake: Using a slant side length as the height instead of the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex.
Correction: The height must be measured at a right angle (90°) to the base. If the triangle is obtuse, the altitude may fall outside the triangle, but it still must be perpendicular to the base line.

results.title: Most Common Geometry Mistakes Students Make (How to Fix Them)
excerpts:
Students know the formula for triangle area is ½ × base × height. The mistake is using a slant side as the height instead of the perpendicular height . The height in the triangle area formula must always be the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex — measured at exactly 90°. It is never a slanted side of the triangle.
❌ Wrong
Triangle with base 10 cm and slant side 7 cm. “Area = ½ × 10 × 7 = 35 cm²”
Using a slant side as height.
✅ Correct
Height must be perpendicular to the base. Look for the right-angle marker (□) on the diagram. Only use that measurement as h.
In area problems, using diameter instead of radius gives an answer that is 4 times too large — because radius is squared.
The Pythagorean theorem (a² + b² = c²) is straightforward in concept, but students make several predictable errors in applying it. The biggest mistake: forgetting that c must always be the hypotenuse — the longest side, opposite the right angle — and not just any side.
The Three Most Common Pythagorean Errors
Error 1 — Adding instead of square-rooting the result:
❌ Wrong
a=3, b=4 → a²+b² = 9+16 = 25 “c = 25”
✅ Correct
c² = 25 “c = √25 = 5 “ Must take the square root!
Error 2 — Using the hypotenuse in the wrong position when finding a shorter side:
❌ Wrong
Hypotenuse = 13, one side = 5 “13² + 5² = c²” → 169+25 = 194 → c = 13.9 ✗
✅ Correct
